title: ffreis metric registry
description: One declarative registry of every number a project publishes. A report's sample gates, its withheld-value states, and the synthetic scenario corpus that proves it works are all projections of this file — never hand-maintained per section. Declaring the metric IS declaring how it can be wrong. Spec: .claude/workspace/reference/every-published-number-is-a-declared-metric.md. The axes exist because each one names an observed way a published number misled a reader: a number with no feeding signal, a count read as a share, a percentile taken over n=1, a section no scenario exercises, and — the one that motivated the standard — a consent-gated sample read as if it were the whole traffic. Semantic conformance beyond this schema is enforced by scripts/validate-metric-registry.py.

$schema.description: Points at this schema so editors validate the registry as you type. Permitted explicitly because `additionalProperties` is false — without this property the documented consumer snippet would be rejected by the schema it names.

name.description: Stable snake_case identifier. Referenced by other entries' `denominator` and `baseline`, and by a scenario's coverage report.

title.description: What a reader of the published surface sees this number called. Keeping it here is what lets an auditor match a rendered label back to its declaration.

kind.description: count=an absolute tally; rate=a part over a whole of the same population (0..1 or a percentage); ratio=a comparison across two different populations; distribution=min/median/percentiles over a sample. rate and ratio need a denominator; distribution needs a minimum sample, because a percentile over one observation is that observation wearing a statistic's name.

surface.description: The published artifact this number appears on — a report name, a dashboard id, an email. One metric may be declared once per surface it appears on, because the same quantity can be honest on one surface and misleading on another.

denominator.description: For kind:rate and kind:ratio — the `name` of the declared metric this one is taken over. Naming it rather than describing it is the point: a reader can follow the reference, and the validator can check it resolves.

baseline.description: For a population that is a SUBSET of the people the surface appears to describe — the `name` of a declared metric whose population is `all-traffic`. Required for `consenting-visitor`: telemetry that only fires after consent cannot measure the visitors who refused it, so it can never be its own denominator, and a reader shown only the consenting sample will read it as the traffic. The baseline is what lets the surface say 'N of about M'.

min_sample.description: The sample size below which this number must be WITHHELD rather than published. Withheld, not omitted: the surface still shows the metric and says the sample was too small, because a silently absent row reads as a zero.

coverage.description: Ids of the scenarios that exercise the signal feeding this metric, so a change that stops it being produced fails something. A metric with neither coverage nor a reasoned `exceptions` entry is vacuous: nothing proves it still works.

seam.description: The ONE code location where this number is computed. Invariant: one metric -> one seam. Two places computing the same published number is how two surfaces come to disagree about the same week.

exceptions.description: Declared, reasoned opt-outs — chiefly 'this metric has no scenario coverage, and here is why'. An exception is a first-class visible allow-list entry, never a silent gap. An entry with no real reason is rejected by scripts/validate-metric-registry.py.

population.description: WHOSE behaviour this number describes. all-traffic=every visit, measured without needing the visitor's cooperation (server logs, edge metrics); consenting-visitor=only visitors who accepted tracking, always a subset of unknown size and so always needs a `baseline`; synthetic=generated by a scenario runner, never a person; internal=owner/developer traffic, deliberately excluded from behavioural reporting; mixed=deliberately spans more than one, which is legitimate for pipeline-health numbers ('is anything arriving at all') and misleading for behavioural ones, so it must say what it mixes in `description`.

signal.description: The event, field or query that feeds this metric — a triad like `form/submit`, a log field, a named query. Specific enough that a reader can tell whether a given record contributes.

excludes.description: Values of the signal deliberately NOT counted (a failed submit is not a conversion). Listing them here is what makes the exclusion reviewable instead of buried in a predicate, and what lets a guard scenario assert it.

store.description: Which store the signal is read from, where a project has more than one. Two stores behind one metric is a known way for the same period to report different numbers.

scope.description: What the exception covers — a named axis, a surface, or a stated condition. Narrow enough that a reader can tell whether a given case falls under it.

reason.description: WHY the requirement does not apply here. A real engineering reason, not a restatement of the scope and not a placeholder — 'TODO'/'N/A'/'later' are rejected by the validator.

added.description: ISO date the exception was granted, so a reader can tell a deliberate long-standing carve-out from fresh debt.
